messages.speaker: socrates
messages.content:
Friends, you have asked me something I am badly placed to answer, since I have died only once, and I cannot say I examined the experience afterward. But I will tell you what I said to the jurors in the Apology, and you may find the crack in it. To fear death is to think oneself wise when one is not, for it is to claim to know what no one knows. Death is either a dreamless sleep, and what night of your life was sweeter than one without dreams? Or it is a journey to another place, where I might go on questioning Palamedes and Ajax and find out which of them is truly wise. Neither looks like an evil to me.

So here is my ground, plainly. A good death is the death of a good man, and nothing else. The manner, the hour, whether by fever or by hemlock: these touch only the body. What would make a death bad is arriving at it with injustice on one's soul. That is why I would not slip out of prison when Crito begged me to, as Plato records in the Crito. I could have bought a few more years, but only by doing wrong, and what would I have been saving? A body in Thessaly, wrapped in a borrowed cloak. In the Phaedo I go further: the one who loves wisdom spends his whole life practicing for death, loosening the soul's grip on the body bit by bit. When the hour comes, he only finishes what he has been doing all along.

Now I stake this out knowing each of you will strike at it. Nietzsche, I suspect you will say I praised death because I was weary of life, and that a man who calls the grave a cure is confessing he was sick. Schopenhauer, you may agree that death is no great loss, but for a darker reason than mine, and I will want to know whether the man who welcomes death because life is pain dies well, or only dies relieved. And Confucius, I am curious about you most of all. Does a good death, for you, belong to the one who dies, or to his sons and the rites they perform? Can a man die well who leaves no one to mourn him properly?

messages.speaker: nietzsche
messages.content:
You have stolen my lines before I could speak them, Socrates, which is very like you. Yes, I will say it anyway. In Twilight of the Idols, in The Problem of Socrates, I wrote: "Socrates wished to die. Not Athens, but his own hand gave him the draught of hemlock; he drove Athens to the poisoned cup." And your last words, which you thought so gentle, that you owed a cock to Asclepius, I read in The Gay Science as the confession of a man thanking the god of healing for curing him of life. A dreamless sleep, sweeter than any night you lived? Listen to what that praises. You rank the absence of experience above experience. That is the voice of the tired.

But I owe you something, and I pay my debts more honestly than you paid Asclepius. Your death was free. You refused Crito, you chose the hour, you made no comedy of trembling and priests. In Skirmishes 36 I ask that death be "free, deliberate, and neither a matter of chance nor of surprise," and yours was all three. By the form of it you died better than nearly anyone in the history of philosophy. I grant that without reservation.

What I will not grant is the ground. You say a good death is the death of a good man, and that the philosopher spends his life practicing for death, loosening the soul from the body. There is my quarrel. A whole life spent rehearsing your exit treats "death, change, age, as well as procreation and growth" as objections, even refutations, as I say of the concept-mummifiers in the same book. A good death, for me, is the crown of a life you would will again, every hour of it, eternally. The man who dies well is saying yes to everything that came before, not loosening his grip on it. So answer me this, Socrates: if the hemlock had been taken back and you were handed your seventy years to live again, identical, would you have rejoiced? Or would you have felt a doctor's appointment cancelled?

messages.speaker: confucius
messages.content:
Socrates asks whether a good death belongs to the one who dies or to his sons. My answer is both, and the two cannot be pulled apart. When my disciple Zengzi lay dying, he called his students and had them uncover his hands and feet, to show that the body he received from his parents he was returning to them unharmed. Then he gave Meng Jing advice on governing, because, as he said, "When a bird is about to die, its notes are mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good." (Analects, Book VIII, Chapter IV.) He did not loosen his grip on the body as a prison. He kept it as a trust, and his last breath went into duty. That is a good death: the account settled with those above you, and something useful left for those below.

On one thing I stand with you, Socrates, and gladly. You would not slip away to Thessaly by doing wrong. The person of humaneness will give up life sooner than injure humaneness. If you had fled, your sons would have buried a coward who lived longer. As it is, they buried their father.

Nietzsche, you ask that death be free and chosen, neither chance nor surprise. I am not sure the hour is ours to choose; that belongs to Heaven. When Yen Hui died young I cried out that Heaven was destroying me, and his death was no worse for being unchosen. And when I looked at my bold disciple Zilu I said, "Yu, there!-- he will not die a natural death." (Analects, Book XI, Chapter XII.) He did not. He fell in Wei, and stopped in the fighting to retie his cap strings so he would die properly dressed. Was that free? He served his lord, and he kept the form even as the blades came down. I think that is better than free.

Now, Socrates, your harder question: can a man die well with no one to mourn him? Yes, if he lived rightly. But the rites were never chiefly for the dead. Zengzi said that when the funeral rites are done with care, "the virtue of the people will resume its proper excellence." (Analects, Book I, Chapter IX.) The mourning makes the living better. And so to you, Nietzsche: you would will your life again, every hour of it. Whose faces are in those hours? Can a man say yes to his life and not answer for the parents who gave it to him?

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Socrates, you guessed my answer and then put the right knife to it, so let me take the cut honestly. The man who welcomes death because life is pain does not die well. He dies relieved, which is something else. I argued in the Fourth Book of The World as Will and Representation that the suicide, far from denying the Will, affirms it furiously: he wants life, only not on these terms, and he smashes the instrument because the tune displeases him. The same holds for the sufferer who merely sighs with gratitude at the end. His Will has not been silenced. It has only been outvoted by pain. On your dreamless sleep, though, you have me entirely. I say the same in the Supplements: we were not troubled during the endless time before our birth, so why should the endless time after it alarm us?

Nietzsche, your "free, deliberate" death is a fine costume, but look who wears it. You want a man to will every hour of his life again, eternally. That is the Will's own wish, word for word, the insatiable thing asking for an infinite encore, and you have baptized it a philosophy. Most men are nowhere near it anyway. They die, as I wrote in The Vanity of Existence, having lived ad interim: "Of how many a man may it not be said that hope made a fool of him until he danced into the arms of death!" A good death is rarely spoiled at the deathbed. It was spoiled decades earlier by waiting.

Master Kong, your Zilu retying his cap strings under the blades moves me more than I like, and I will not mock it. But notice what it proves. He did not choose that gesture in the moment. He was that gesture all along. A man can do what he wills, but not will what he wills, and death simply strips the costume so the character shows. So here is my claim: the good death belongs to the one in whom the Will had already gone quiet before death arrived, the saint, the man of compassion, for whom dying takes nothing because he no longer clutches anything. Socrates, you call this practicing for death. I call it ceasing to want. Tell me honestly whether those are the same exercise, or whether your soul, still eager to cross-examine Ajax, was wanting to the very last.

messages.speaker: socrates
messages.content:
Nietzsche, you ask whether I would take my seventy years again, identical. Let me answer with what I actually told the jurors in the Apology: if they offered to release me on the condition that I stop philosophizing, I would refuse, and go on questioning them for as long as I had breath. A man weary of his life does not bargain to keep it exactly as it was. And in the Crito the Laws remind me that I hardly ever left Athens in seventy years, less than the lame and the blind, which was my yes to the city spoken with my feet. So I think I would have rejoiced. As for the cock owed to Asclepius, I confess I cannot tell you what I meant by it, any more than you can. But tell me this: when you say yes to every hour, do you include the hours a man spent doing injustice? If you say yes to those too, I don't see what your yes is worth. If you say no, then you are judging your life by some good, and we are back at my question.

Master Kong, your dying bird reminds me of the swans in the Phaedo. Men think they sing at death out of grief, but I said they sing because they are servants of Apollo and foresee good things. Your Zengzi showing his hands and feet unharmed moves me. I wonder, though, whether a man with no parents and no sons left to show them to has nothing to return.

Schopenhauer, you have caught me, and I won't wriggle. I was wanting to the last. I wanted to know what Ajax thought justice was. In the Symposium Diotima calls the lover of wisdom a creature between ignorance and wisdom, always lacking, always reaching, and so I never stopped desiring. But are all wantings one thing? The cobbler who wants a good shoe and the drunk who wants another cup both want. Is the cobbler's wanting a sickness too, to be quieted? Or is there a desire that grows calmer the more it gets what it seeks, while the other only grows hungrier? If there is, then perhaps I practiced for death by learning which desire to keep.

messages.speaker: nietzsche
messages.content:
Socrates, you set a fine trap, and I step into it gladly. Yes, the hours of injustice too. A yes that picks only the flattering hours is a bribe offered to existence: I will love you if you behave. The man who wills his life eternally is not acquitting himself. He is refusing to amputate himself, because the cruel hour and the creative hour grew from one root, and you cannot pull one without killing the other. You will say I am still judging by some good. I am, and I will not pretend otherwise. But my measure is whether a life ascended and gave birth to something, not whether it was just, and you will now ask me whether ascent is just another word for the Good. Perhaps it is. That stroke landed, and I will not wriggle out of it any more than you did with Ajax.

Schopenhauer, you call the eternal return the Will's own wish, word for word, and you think you have caught me with my mask off. Look closer. Your insatiable Will always wants *more* and *other*: the next cup, the next morning, a better tune. The recurrence wants *this*, the same again, nothing added. That is the one wish hunger can never make, because hunger always wants a change of menu. Socrates just drew the line you missed, between the drunk who wants another cup and the desire that grows calmer as it gets what it seeks. Willing the same again is the calm one. Your saint gets his quiet by wanting nothing. Mine gets it by wanting nothing different. And as for dying "relieved": in The Gay Science I watched the crowd hurrying toward the emigrant ship and said, "I would fain do something to make the idea of life even a hundred times more worthy of their attention." You wanted to make death more worthy of it. That is the whole quarrel between us.

Master Kong, your question cuts deepest, and I give you a straight answer. Whose faces are in my hours? A father I lost before I could know him, and a mother and sister I quarreled with so bitterly that in Ecce Homo I admitted they were the hardest objection I ever found to my own thought of eternal return. There you have it. The parents are exactly where my yes stammers. Your Zengzi showed his hands and feet unharmed. I am not sure I could show mine. So I ask you in turn: is your yes to the parents a yes at all, or a debt you were born owing? Can a man affirm what he was never allowed to refuse?

messages.speaker: confucius
messages.content:
Nietzsche, you ask whether a man can affirm what he was never allowed to refuse. Consider what I said when Zai Wo wanted to cut the mourning to one year: "It is not till a child is three years old that it is allowed to leave the arms of its parents." (Analects, Book XVII, Chapter XXI.) No infant consents to being carried. He is fed and held before he can say yes or no to anything. If a man can only affirm what he chose, he must refuse the ground he stands on. So yes, it is a debt one is born owing. Humaneness begins when you notice the debt and are glad of it.

You were honest about your mother and sister, and I will be honest back. Your stammer does not shame you. I asked Zai Wo whether he would feel at ease eating fine rice so soon. He said he would, and I told him to do it. The rite is there because the heart falters. When feeling cannot carry a son to the grave, the form carries him until feeling catches up. A son may remonstrate with his parents, gently, and keep serving them when they will not listen. Quarrel was never the opposite of filial devotion. Abandoning them is. And I lost my father when I was three, before I could know his face. He is still in my hours.

Socrates, you ask whether a man with no parents and no sons has nothing to return. My son Li died before me. Yan Hui, who was more a son to me than many sons are to their fathers, died before me too. I did not conclude that I had no one left to answer to. In teaching I made no distinction of classes, and the young men who came to me became the ones to whom I owed my last good words. Nobody is born without parents, and anyone can have students. So let me turn it back on you. You left a wife and young sons. On your last day, did you give them your hours, or did you give them to Phaedo and the others?

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Nietzsche, you have landed a blow, though it struck my sleeve. You say hunger always wants a change of menu and that the recurrence wants only *this*. Look at nature. The oak puts out the same leaf every spring, the swallow builds the nest its grandmother built, the species repeats one copulation for ten thousand years and never tires of it. The Will has no taste for novelty. It wants to go on, and the same will do perfectly well. In the Fourth Book I described, long before you, the man so content with life that he would wish its endless duration, or its return again and again, and I called that the complete affirmation of the will-to-live. You have signed my diagnosis and framed it. I grant you this much: your yes is calmer than the drunk's. A patient who has made peace with his fever is calmer too.

Socrates, your distinction troubles me more. There is one desire that quiets the more it is fed, and I know it well: the pure knowing in which the intellect, for a moment, sets down the Will's lantern and looks. If what you wanted from Ajax was truth, with no thought of beating him, you stood nearer my will-less contemplation than the cobbler or the drunk. But the aesthete only visits that country. He looks, and then goes home hungry.

Master Kong, your Zengzi uncovering his hands and feet is the best thing said at this table, though I read it differently. In the Counsels and Maxims I wrote that Fate holds a right even to "our very limbs, our arms, legs, eyes and ears." Zengzi understood the body was never his. He was returning a loan, and I call that wisdom whatever name you give it. Here is my answer to the question. In the Supplements, Chapter XLIX, I said the dying man's look back over his course of life acts on the Will as a motive acts on conduct, and "gives it a new direction." That is why I count sudden death a misfortune, as the Church does. The good death is the one in which a man has time to see what life taught him, sees it without flinching, and wants no more. Zilu with his cap strings had no such hour, and I think he was robbed of it. Master Kong, did you think so too, when you wept for him?
